units.title: Demonstrations, behavior cloning and action likelihoods
outcomes: Derive the behavior-cloning likelihood for discrete and continuous actions and implement it from a blank file.
Choose an action distribution (logits, Gaussian parameters, or an expressive generative head) and defend the choice on multimodal data.
Build a demonstration baseline with recorded data identity that later offline methods must beat.
units.why: Behavior cloning is the baseline every offline method must beat. It needs no reward and no interaction, so its failure modes set the terms for everything later in this section.

next.note: Show where this baseline breaks under its own state distribution.
Record the dataset identity this baseline depends on.

study.title: Lecture 2: Behavioral Cloning, from MLE to the BC algorithm
study.locator: Part 1, maximum likelihood as supervised learning (PDF pp. 2-8); Part 2, demonstration trajectories and the ALVINN behavior-cloning algorithm (PDF pp. 9-12)

study.title: The behavior-cloning objective
study.locator: Section 1.1: discrete cross-entropy versus continuous MSE and negative log-likelihood, with the worked p = 0.7 versus p = 0.95 loss example (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 02: expressive policy distributions
study.locator: PDF pp. 6-21: the mean-of-modes failure of regression, generative policy heads, diffusion and flow matching, action chunking, and the unimodal versus multimodal summary
study.depth: Stop before PDF p. 23. Compounding errors and DAgger belong to the next unit.

study.title: Lecture 3: action distributions for imitation
study.locator: PDF pp. 9-16: autoregressive discretization, expressive continuous distributions, flow matching, and action chunking

focus: Behavior cloning is maximum likelihood on expert pairs. Discrete actions use logits with cross-entropy; continuous actions use distribution parameters with MSE or negative log-likelihood.
A single number pins the loss scale: \(-\log 0.7 = 0.357\) versus \(-\log 0.95 = 0.051\). Recompute both before trusting any training curve.
An MSE head predicts the conditional mean. On multimodal demonstrations (two experts, two modes) the mean can be an action no expert took.

Stanford Homework 1 fixes the control interface: policies predict a chunk of \(20\) future targets and execute the first \(10\) before replanning. The loss averages over the chunk; control uses only its head.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the categorical behavior-cloning gradient from the log policy term, evaluate the two NLL values above, and state which part of a Stanford Homework 1 action chunk the loss sees and which part the rollout executes.
traps: Reading a falling validation loss as a working policy. Likelihood is measured under the expert state distribution; closed-loop return is measured under the learner's own distribution, and the two can disagree sharply.
Fitting MSE to multimodal demonstrations and shipping the mean action. Check the action histogram first; a mean between two modes is a new, untested behavior.
Tuning the chunk length as if it were only a loss detail. It also sets the open-loop execution horizon, so it changes the control problem, not just the gradient.

selfTest.q: Write the behavior-cloning objective and name the loss for discrete and for continuous unimodal actions.
selfTest.a: Maximize the expected log probability of expert actions under the data. Discrete: cross-entropy over logits. Continuous unimodal: MSE or Gaussian negative log-likelihood over distribution parameters.

selfTest.q: A policy assigns probability 0.7 to the expert action on one state and 0.95 on another. What is each negative log-likelihood?
selfTest.a: 0.357 and 0.051. Higher expert probability means lower loss, and the scale is logarithmic, not linear.

selfTest.q: Two demonstrators pass an obstacle on opposite sides. What does an MSE behavior-cloning policy do at the obstacle, and why is it wrong?
selfTest.a: It predicts the mean action, straight at the obstacle, which neither demonstrator took. The fix is an expressive multimodal head such as a mixture, diffusion, or flow-matching policy.

selfTest.q: Stanford Homework 1 uses an action chunk of 20 with 10 executed steps. What does the policy output, and what does the rollout use?
selfTest.a: It outputs 20 future target positions and executes the first 10 open-loop before re-querying the policy. This receding-horizon control separates the loss horizon from the execution horizon.

practice.name: Berkeley CS 285 Homework 1: Imitation Learning (MSE and flow-matching policies)
practice.locator: Implement `MSEPolicy` and `FlowMatchingPolicy` in `src/hw1_imitation/model.py` plus the loop in `src/hw1_imitation/train.py`; pass thresholds are reward 0.5 (MSE) and 0.7 (flow). Handout: https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/static/homeworks/hw1.pdf

units.title: Covariate shift, compounding imitation error and DAgger
outcomes: Derive the quadratic compounding bound for offline imitation and the linear bound with interactive queries.
Run the DAgger loop (roll out learner, label visited states with the expert, aggregate, retrain) and state exactly what the extra queries change.
Tell covariate shift apart from causal confusion and from fixed-dataset offline limits.
units.why: A 1 percent mistake rate sounds safe until the horizon multiplies it. This unit makes the horizon dependence quantitative and shows what only an interactive expert can fix.

next.note: See what interaction buys when no expert labels exist at all.
Face the same shift with no expert to query.

study.title: Lecture 2: how bad covariate shift can be, then DAgger
study.locator: Part 4, the mistake analysis with the quadratic horizon dependence (PDF pp. 23-32); Part 5, DAgger dataset aggregation and the common-variant question (PDF pp. 33-38)

study.title: DAgger: the reduction and the aggregation loop
study.locator: Sections 1-3: the supervised T-squared mistake argument, forward training with Theorem 2.2, SMILe mixing, and the Section 3 dataset-aggregation loop that trains a stationary deterministic policy

study.title: Lecture 02: compounding errors and interventions
study.locator: PDF pp. 23-26: the covariate-shift diagram, the corrective-data loop (dataset aggregation), and human-gated DAgger
study.depth: Use pp. 7-22 only as background from the previous unit. The examinable material here is pp. 23-26.

study.title: Why cloning errors compound, and the DAgger fix
study.locator: Sections 2 and 3: the error-rate table (1 percent error at horizons 10, 50, 100, 1000) and the mixing schedule with expert relabeling of policy-visited states (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: The arithmetic first: at 1 percent error per step, clean-run probability is \(0.99^{10} = 0.90\) but \(0.99^{100} = 0.37\) and \(0.99^{1000} = 0.00004\). Recompute all three.

The bound behind it: offline cloning pays up to \(O(T^2 \epsilon)\), because one off-distribution step can cost the rest of the horizon; labeling the learner's own visited states cuts it to \(O(T \epsilon)\).
DAgger aggregates policy-visited states with expert labels and retrains on the union. The load-bearing ingredient is the expert label on the learner's distribution, not the extra states alone.

DAgger needs an interactive expert, so it does not apply to a fixed offline dataset. Causal confusion is a separate failure: Berkeley Lecture 3 asks whether history or DAgger mitigates it, citing de Haan et al., who find that more input information can make cloning worse and resolve it with targeted interventions.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the three clean-run probabilities above, state both bounds with the one-step-leaves-distribution intuition, and write the four DAgger steps (roll out learner, query expert on visited states, aggregate, retrain).
traps: Believing more clean demonstrations remove the quadratic term. They shrink the per-step rate but the horizon dependence stays; recoveries in the data (the Lecture 2 paradox) can help more than extra clean runs.

Running the common intervention variant (the human takes over at some step and only the takeover data is stored) and quoting the DAgger guarantee. Labels then cover the takeover states and what the human drives afterwards, not every state the learner visits; Lecture 2 poses exactly this question.
Treating DAgger as an offline algorithm. It needs an interactive expert during training; with only a fixed dataset you are back in the offline regime of the next units.

selfTest.q: At 1 percent per-step error, what fraction of length-100 runs stays clean, and why does length-1000 collapse?
selfTest.a: 0.37 for length 100; 0.00004 for length 1000. Clean probability decays exponentially as 0.99^T, so long horizons need a far smaller per-step rate.

selfTest.q: State the offline cloning bound and the DAgger bound, and the intuition for the gap.
selfTest.a: Offline: \(O(T^2 \epsilon)\); interactive: \(O(T \epsilon)\). Offline, one mistake can leave the training distribution and cost \(O(T)\) more mistakes, and there are \(T\) chances to leave; on-policy labels remove the distribution mismatch.

selfTest.q: What exactly is added to the dataset at each DAgger iteration?
selfTest.a: States visited by the current learner policy, each labeled with the expert's action, appended to all previous data. The next policy mimics the expert on the whole aggregate.

selfTest.q: Demonstrations show braking whenever the dashboard brake indicator is lit, because braking turns it on. Why can a cloned policy brake at the wrong time, and why is this not covariate shift?
selfTest.a: The indicator is an effect of braking that predicts the expert action almost perfectly, so the policy can key on it instead of the road: causal confusion. More data from the same distribution keeps cue and action together; de Haan et al. resolve it with targeted interventions, environment interaction or expert queries, and compare against DAgger, so do not assume aggregation alone fixes it.

practice.name: Stanford CS224R Homework 1, Problem 3: DAgger on Flappy Bird
practice.locator: Problem 3: implement `DeterministicExpert.act`, rollout, and relabel in `dagger.py`, retrain with the Problem 1 regression objective, and submit `dagger_hard.txt` against `bc_reg_hard.txt`
practice.note: Runs on CPU or Colab. Compare hard-mode success before and after aggregation, and state what the expert queries added. Follow the Stanford honor code; generative-model code is banned for this homework.

fit.note: Berkeley Lecture 2 plus Stanford Lecture 02 cover shift and DAgger at derive depth, the DAgger paper supplies the bounds, and Stanford HW1 gives checked practice.

units.title: Inverse RL, the reward-learning boundary, GAIL and occupancy matching
outcomes: Explain why demonstrations underdetermine the reward and where maximum-entropy IRL pays for its answer.
State GAIL as occupancy matching (Jensen-Shannon via the discriminator game) and what it recovers instead of a reward.
Say what GAIL needs that behavior cloning does not, and read its discriminator signs correctly.
units.why: Some tasks have demonstrations but no reward function. This unit draws the boundary: what reward learning can identify, and what occupancy matching settles for instead.

next.note: Return to fixed data, where neither expert queries nor rollouts exist.
See how offline methods use rewards where imitation cannot.

study.title: Inverse RL and GAIL
study.locator: Sections 1 and 2: the inverse-RL setting, the maximum-entropy distribution over trajectories, and why the partition function is intractable; Section 3: the discriminator-policy alternation and the occupancy-ratio optimum (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the page for the setting and the game structure. Take proposition numbers and the saddle objective from the paper below, not from this pre-reading.

study.title: GAIL: occupancy matching and the discriminator game
study.locator: Sections 3-5 of arXiv:1606.03476v1: the occupancy measure with Propositions 3.1 and 3.2, the Jensen-Shannon matching objective with Equations 15-18, and Algorithm 1 with the TRPO policy step

study.title: Comparing BC, DAgger, and GAIL
study.locator: Section 4: interaction, label, and reward requirements side by side (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Inverse RL is underspecified: many rewards, including zero, rationalize the same demonstrations. Maximum entropy selects the trajectory distribution proportional to exponentiated return, but its partition function sums over all trajectories and is intractable.

GAIL stops asking for a reward and matches occupancy measures instead: the policy whose state-action visitation minimizes Jensen-Shannon divergence to the expert's. What it recovers is a policy, not a transferable reward.

The paper's saddle (Equation 16) puts the log discriminator term on learner samples and the log one-minus term on expert samples, with policy cost equal to log discriminator output. Other sources flip this labeling, so check which expectation gets which term before reading any discriminator value.
The 2016 TRPO policy step inside Algorithm 1 is dated machinery. Learn the objective and the alternation; a modern implementation would use a newer policy optimizer.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the occupancy measure, the Equation 16 saddle with each term labeled by its sampling policy, and the one-line reason IRL cannot promise a unique reward.
traps: Reading a discriminator output of 0.8 as expert-like without checking the labeling. Under the paper's Equation 16, the log term sits on learner samples, so a high value means looks-like-learner; flipped labelings mean the opposite.
Calling GAIL an offline algorithm. It samples fresh learner trajectories every iteration (Algorithm 1, line 3), so it needs environment interaction that fixed-dataset methods do not have.
Expecting the learned discriminator to serve as a reward for new tasks. It is a local cost tied to this expert and this training run, not an identified reward function.

selfTest.q: Why can inverse RL never promise the true reward, even with infinite demonstrations?
selfTest.a: Demonstrations constrain behavior, not reward: many rewards produce the same optimal policy. Maximum entropy picks one by an entropy criterion, and its partition function is intractable, so approximations choose further.

selfTest.q: In the paper's Equation 16, which samples does the log discriminator term average over, and what does a high discriminator value mean?
selfTest.a: Learner-policy samples average the log term; expert samples average the log one-minus term. High means the pair looks like the learner under this labeling, the reverse of pages that put the expert under the log term.

selfTest.q: What does GAIL need that behavior cloning does not, and what does it recover instead of a reward?
selfTest.a: Environment interaction for fresh learner rollouts plus expert samples each iteration. It recovers an imitator policy whose occupancy matches the expert's, not a reward function.

selfTest.q: Is the TRPO step load-bearing for the GAIL idea?
selfTest.a: No. The idea is the occupancy-matching objective and the discriminator game. TRPO is the 2016 optimizer; the objective survives a change of policy optimizer.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a discriminator-versus-occupancy check that trains a classifier on expert-versus-learner pairs from logged data, reports its optimum under the stated labeling, and states the online rollouts GAIL would still need beyond the offline data.
units.stopWhen: You can write the occupancy definition and the saddle from memory with correct term labels, and state in one sentence each what IRL cannot identify and what interaction GAIL requires.

fit.note: The Hands-on pages plus GAIL Sections 3-5 cover the reward-learning boundary and occupancy matching at explain depth; no runnable GAIL exists in the pool, so practice goes to the mini-project.

units.title: Offline datasets, behavior-policy identity, coverage and quality sweeps
outcomes: Record behavior-policy identity (dataset id, version, collection policy) with every offline result.
Diagnose coverage and support gaps, including counterfactual queries the data cannot answer.
Run quality, diversity, and coverage sweeps that compare cloning against an offline RL method with online truth reserved for audit.
units.why: Offline data cannot be repaired by interaction. Coverage and identity decide what any later algorithm is allowed to conclude, so this unit builds the dataset discipline first.

next.note: See what goes wrong when training queries outside this coverage.
Weigh what the logging policy actually supports.

study.title: What offline RL is and why it is hard
study.locator: Sections 2.2 and 2.4 of arXiv:2005.01643v3: the offline problem statement with the behavior policy, then distributional shift named as the fundamental challenge

study.title: Lecture 17: counterfactual queries and the SAC overestimation demo
study.locator: PDF pp. 10-11: training data versus what the policy wants to do, with unseen actions as the counterfactual question; PDF p. 17: the soft actor-critic demo where predicted values exceed achieved returns on a log scale; PDF p. 18: why online sampling error becomes worse offline

study.title: Minari dataset standards and one versioned dataset
study.locator: Dataset Standards: episode and step data, spaces, and versioning; then open one hosted set such as https://minari.farama.org/datasets/mujoco/invertedpendulum/expert-v0/ and record its id, version, episode and step counts, and action bounds (pages read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 07: the offline process and the behavior policy
study.locator: PDF pp. 7-9: training on a static dataset sampled from an unknown behavior policy that may mix human, scripted, and prior-RL sources
study.depth: Read pp. 7-9 only here. Stitching and the method ideas belong to later units.

focus: The behavior policy may be a mixture (human plus scripted plus prior runs) and is often unknown. Record the dataset id and version with every result; a result without them is not reproducible.
A counterfactual query asks the value of an action never taken in that state. Online methods answer by trying it; offline methods must flag it, constrain around it, or admit they cannot answer.
Expert data is narrow by construction. Medium or diverse data often trains better offline policies because coverage and stitching matter more than demonstration quality.

Design sweeps as dataset variant by algorithm: at least two dataset types (for example expert versus medium) crossed with cloning versus one offline RL method, with online returns reserved for audit only.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, fetch one Minari dataset record and write down its id, version, episode and step counts, and action bounds; then sketch the variant-by-algorithm sweep table with the audit-only column marked.
traps: Equating more transitions with more coverage. Ten million steps from one deterministic policy cover one thin manifold; diversity of behavior is the coverage, not the row count.
Downloading a dataset without its version and calling the experiment reproducible. Hosted sets are versioned because their contents change; the id alone does not pin the bytes.
Tuning on online returns and calling the study offline. Online ground truth audits estimators after selection; the moment it guides a choice, the offline claim is void.

selfTest.q: What four facts must accompany every offline result, and why?
selfTest.a: Dataset id, dataset version, behavior-policy description, and environment version. Without them nobody can tell what distribution the numbers came from or reproduce the bytes.

selfTest.q: Why can medium-quality diverse data beat expert data for offline RL?
selfTest.a: Expert data concentrates on one narrow behavior, so new policies quickly leave its support. Diverse data covers more states and actions, which lets stitching and conservative methods compose better-than-demonstrator behavior.

selfTest.q: What is a counterfactual query, and what did the Lecture 17 soft actor-critic demo show about it?
selfTest.a: Asking whether an unseen action is good without data to check. The demo showed predicted Q-values massively above achieved returns on a log scale: the policy asked, the data could not answer, and the values were wrong.

selfTest.q: What belongs in the audit-only column of your sweep table?
selfTest.a: Online returns computed after all selection is finished, used only to judge estimators and methods. Nothing in that column may change a hyperparameter or a choice.

practice.name: Minari tutorial: behavioral cloning with PyTorch

units.title: Extrapolation error, pessimism and Conservative Q-Learning
outcomes: Locate where extrapolation error enters a Bellman backup and demonstrate it with a fixed-batch query.
Derive the Conservative Q-Learning regularizer and the lower-bound claims behind it.
Sweep the conservatism weight and show lowered out-of-data values with in-data values held.
units.why: Standard backups query actions the data never saw and believe the answer. Pessimism is the fix that keeps offline values honest, and CQL is its cleanest expression.

next.note: Avoid out-of-data queries altogether instead of penalizing them.
See what conservative values cost when interaction resumes.

study.title: Shift in dynamic programming, uncertainty, and CQL
study.locator: Sections 4.2 through 4.5 of arXiv:2005.01643v3: distributional shift inside Bellman backups, policy constraints, uncertainty-based conservative estimates, and the CQL penalty as conservatism without explicit uncertainty

study.title: CQL: the regularizer and the lower bounds
study.locator: Sections 1-3 of arXiv:2006.04779v3: Equations 1 and 2 with Theorems 3.1 (pointwise lower bound under support conditions) and 3.2 (tighter expected-value bound that is not pointwise); Section 3.2: the CQL(H) log-sum-exp variant (Equation 4), with Section 4 for the practical algorithm

study.title: Lecture 18: Conservative Q-Learning slides
study.locator: PDF pp. 17-21: pushing down large Q-values while pushing up in-data pairs, with the policy-constraint versus pessimism framing from PDF p. 2
study.depth: Use pp. 17-21 only here. IQL (pp. 11-15) and offline-to-online (pp. 22-24) belong to other units.

study.title: CQL against BCQ and IQL
study.locator: Sections 2.2 and 2.4: the log-sum-exp soft maximum over all actions, the in-data restoration term, the penalty gap, and the method comparison table (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Extrapolation error enters at the max: a Q-learning backup queries values at actions the dataset never paired with that state, and the maximizer seeks out exactly the overestimated ones.

CQL adds a penalty with two opposing terms: push down a soft maximum over all actions and push up the pairs actually observed. The gap between them is the conservatism; the paper's theory turns it into a lower bound.
A concrete gap: in-data value \(5\) with one unseen action at \(8\) gives a soft maximum of \(8.05\) and a pre-weight gap of \(3.05\). Recompute both numbers; the weight in front sets the strength.

The two theorems differ in scope: Equation 1 gives a pointwise lower bound when the pushed-down distribution stays inside behavior support; Equation 2 gives a tighter bound on expected policy value that does not hold pointwise.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the CQL(H) objective (Bellman error plus the weighted soft-maximum minus in-data term), compute the 8.05 and 3.05 values above, and implement the fixed-batch regularizer showing out-of-data values falling while in-data values hold.
traps: Quoting the lower bound for arbitrary actions. The pointwise claim needs the support condition of Theorem 3.1; the Equation 2 form bounds expected value only, and neither survives truly unsupported queries.

Setting the conservatism weight once and forgetting it. The paper trades performance against conservatism through this weight and notes that the weight needed for the lower bound falls as data grows; sweep it, do not copy it.
Assuming conservatism is free at deployment time. Pushed-down values cause the initial unlearning dip when online fine-tuning starts; that measurement belongs to the sequence-models unit.

selfTest.q: Where exactly does extrapolation error enter a Q-learning backup?
selfTest.a: At the maximization (or argmax-action query) over next actions: it evaluates the Q-function at actions the dataset never paired with that state, and maximization selects the most overestimated one.

selfTest.q: In-data value 5, one unseen action valued 8. What are the soft maximum and the penalty gap?
selfTest.a: Soft maximum 8.05, gap 3.05 before the weight. The soft maximum is dominated by the unseen 8, which is exactly the overestimation the penalty must suppress.

selfTest.q: Contrast the two CQL theorems in one sentence each.
selfTest.a: Theorem 3.1: iterating the Equation 1 update lower-bounds the true Q pointwise when the penalty distribution stays in behavior support. Theorem 3.2: the Equation 2 form gives a tighter bound on expected policy value but not a pointwise bound.

selfTest.q: What should happen to the conservatism weight as the dataset grows toward infinite coverage?
selfTest.a: The weight needed for the lower bound shrinks: the paper notes that as \(|\mathcal{D}(s, a)|\) grows the required weight decreases, so in the limit of infinite data an extremely small weight suffices.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a fixed-batch CQL regularizer test that lowers Q-values on actions the dataset does not contain while holding in-data values, plus a conservatism-weight sweep with the tradeoff written down.
units.stopWhen: You derive the regularizer from memory, reproduce the 8.05 gap on paper, and can state which theorem covers which claim without hedging.

fit.note: The CQL paper plus the survey and both course treatments cover extrapolation and pessimism at derive depth; no runnable CQL exists in the pool, so the fixed-batch test goes to the mini-project.

units.title: Implicit Q-Learning expectiles and advantage-weighted actor updates
outcomes: Derive the expectile value loss, the Q target, and the advantage-weighted policy update from the IQL paper.
Explain why the separate value function avoids both out-of-data queries and lucky-transition bias.
Compare IQL with cloning across dataset quality and coverage, sweeping the expectile.
units.why: IQL learns multi-step values without ever asking the Q-function about unseen actions. It is the method that makes the no-OOD-query idea concrete and testable on a fixed batch.

next.note: Compare multi-step stitching against sequence copying.
See where even IQL cannot select without coverage.

study.title: IQL: expectiles, the Q backup, and policy extraction
study.locator: Sections 4.1-4.3 of arXiv:2110.06169v1: expectile regression with Figure 1, the value loss and Q loss, the advantage-weighted extraction with Algorithm 1; Section 5.1: one-step improvement versus multi-step IQL

study.title: Lecture 07: advantage weighting to expectile IQL
study.locator: PDF pp. 20-21: full advantage-weighted regression; PDF p. 25: the expectile loss with its worked plot; PDF p. 26: the three IQL losses with the Homework 3 pointer
study.depth: Watch the notation: the slides write the expectile weight as a small value below 0.5 where the paper and the homework write it above 0.5. They are complements of each other; the traps below pin this down.

study.title: Lecture 18: implicit constraints to IQL
study.locator: PDF pp. 9-10: advantage-weighted regression and the AWAC update; PDF pp. 11-15: avoiding all out-of-distribution actions in the Q update with the expectile value function

study.title: IQL and how it differs from AWAC
study.locator: Sections 2.3, 3.2, and 3.3: the expectile backup through next-state values instead of maximized Q, and the AWAC-versus-IQL advantage comparison (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: The three losses use dataset actions only: an expectile value loss that estimates an upper envelope over in-support actions, a mean-squared Q loss backed up through next-state values, and an advantage-weighted cloning loss for the policy.

The separate value function does two jobs at once: it never queries unseen actions, and it averages out transition luck, because a high target from a lucky next state does not move the action-envelope estimate the way a directly fitted maximum would.

The expectile parameter is a sweep, not a constant: 0.5 recovers the mean and higher values reach further toward the in-support maximum. The homework compares 0.2 against 0.9 on the U-maze for exactly this reason.

AWAC and IQL share the weighted-cloning policy form but estimate advantage differently: AWAC backs advantages through a standard Q backup that still queries next actions sampled from the current policy, while IQL backs them through the expectile value with no out-of-data query.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write all three IQL losses, compute the 0.9 expectile of the values 0, 0, and 10 (8.18, above the mean 3.33), and show on a fixed batch that no loss term evaluates an action outside the dataset.
traps: Mixing up the expectile conventions. The paper and both homeworks write the upper expectile above 0.5 (0.9 beats 0.2 for reaching good values); the Stanford slides write the same loss with the complement below 0.5. Convert before comparing numbers across sources.

Treating the expectile as a maximum. It approaches the in-support maximum as the parameter tends to 1 but stays an expectile of dataset values at any fixed setting; it never invents out-of-support actions.

Reading small inverse temperature as aggressive. In the extraction loss, small temperature behaves like plain cloning and large temperature reaches for the Q maximum; the direction is the reverse of a penalty weight.

selfTest.q: Compute the 0.9 expectile of values 0, 0, and 10, and compare with the mean.
selfTest.a: 8.18, above the mean 3.33. The minimizer weights the above-estimate squared error at 0.9 and the below-estimate part at 0.1, pulling the estimate toward the high in-support value.

selfTest.q: Why does IQL fit a separate value function instead of taking expectiles of Q targets directly?
selfTest.a: A high Q target can come from a lucky transition into a good state rather than a good action. The separate value function takes the expectile over actions only, while the Q backup averages over transition stochasticity.

selfTest.q: Where does AWAC still query out-of-distribution actions while IQL does not?
selfTest.a: AWAC's advantage comes from a standard Bellman backup that samples next actions from the current policy, which may be unseen. IQL's backup goes through the expectile of dataset values at the next state, using dataset actions only.

selfTest.q: What does the extraction loss become as the inverse temperature goes to zero?
selfTest.a: Plain behavior cloning: all advantage weights tend to 1, so every dataset action is imitated equally regardless of value.

selfTest.q: A run with expectile 0.2 underperforms 0.9 on the U-maze. What does that tell you, in one sentence?
selfTest.a: The task needs multi-step improvement toward good in-support values, which the near-mean estimate cannot provide; the higher expectile reaches further up the dataset's value envelope.

practice.name: Stanford CS224R Homework 3, Questions 1-2: AWAC and IQL on AntMaze

fit.note: The IQL paper plus both course treatments cover expectiles and weighted extraction at derive depth, and Stanford HW3 gives named AWAC and IQL practice.

units.title: The sequence-modeling view and online fine-tuning after offline initialization
outcomes: Explain the sequence-modeling view (return-conditioned action prediction) and its stitching limit.
State the calibration condition that prevents initial unlearning when online fine-tuning starts.
Measure the first online episodes after offline initialization with and without the calibration fix.
units.why: Offline training ends and interaction resumes. This unit decides whether the offline initialization helps or gets unlearned first, and where sequence copying stops being reinforcement learning.

next.note: Select among fine-tuned candidates without spending online truth.
Guard the handoff with normalization, fallback, and audit.

study.title: Offline RL through sequence modeling
study.locator: Sections 1.1-1.5: return-to-go conditioning, supervised action prediction, the inference loop that decrements the target return, why the method can work, and its limitations including stitching (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 07: stitching and the imitation baselines
study.locator: PDF pp. 11-12: the stitching diagram (good segments recombined into a better whole); PDF p. 17: filtered imitation that copies only good trajectories; PDF p. 28: the summary listing filtered and weighted imitation as baselines, with trajectory stitching as the improvement over imitation

study.title: Cal-QL: calibration against the initial dip
study.locator: Sections 1 and 4.1 of arXiv:2303.05479v4: the initial unlearning diagnosis for conservative methods; Section 4.2 with Definition 4.1 (calibration of the learned values against a reference policy); Section 7: the fine-tuning experiments that measure the first online episodes

study.title: Lecture 18: the offline-to-online problem
study.locator: PDF pp. 22-25: offline pretraining followed by fast online fine-tuning, the CQL recovery period wasted regaining offline performance, and why one algorithm that does both phases well is hard to find

focus: A Decision Transformer is supervised learning on triples: condition on a target return, predict the action, then subtract the observed reward from the target at the next step. No Bellman backup ever combines two different trajectories.

Stitching is the test sequence models fail: one dataset segment runs from start to middle, another from middle to goal, and only multi-step dynamic programming returns the full route. Copying whole trajectories, however filtered, cannot invent the combination.

Calibration is a one-sided guard, not accuracy: expected learned values must sit above the reference policy's values on dataset states. Conservative pretraining violates it by pushing learned-policy values too far down, so online updates spend their first episodes unlearning.
The measurement that matters is the return curve of the first online episodes with and without the calibration fix, not the asymptotic return after both converge.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the return-conditioned inference loop (set target, act, subtract reward, repeat) and the calibration inequality, then sketch the two-segment stitching diagram and mark which methods cross the gap.
traps: Conditioning on a high target return and calling the result optimal. An unreachable target pushes the model into trajectory regions it never saw; sequence models copy statistics, they do not optimize.

Assuming fine-tuning can only help. Conservative initialization starts below the behavior it already had, so early online training first recovers lost performance; skipping the first-episode measurement hides exactly this cost.
Reading calibration as value accuracy. It bounds learned values from below against a reference; a calibrated function can still be far from the true values everywhere.

selfTest.q: Write the Decision Transformer inference loop in three steps.
selfTest.a: Set a target return and condition the policy on it with the history; execute the predicted action and observe the reward; subtract the reward from the remaining target and repeat until the episode ends.

selfTest.q: Why can filtered cloning plus a high target still fail the stitching diagram?
selfTest.a: Filtering copies only good whole trajectories, and no dataset trajectory contains the combined route. Without a Bellman backup joining the segments at the shared middle, the combination is never constructed.

selfTest.q: State the calibration condition and what breaks when it fails.
selfTest.a: Expected learned values under the learned policy must exceed the reference policy's values on dataset states. When conservative pretraining pushes them below, online updates first unlearn the initialization before improving it.

selfTest.q: What is the load-bearing measurement when comparing a calibrated against an uncalibrated fine-tuning run?
selfTest.a: Returns over the first online episodes: whether the dip appears, how deep it is, and how many episodes recalibration costs, before any asymptotic comparison.

practice.name: Stanford CS224R Homework 3, Question 3: the stitching study
practice.locator: Question 3: IQL versus Filtered BC on the PointMass task with suboptimal data; report which method improves over the dataset behavior and explain the gap in terms of value estimation
practice.note: Runs on Modal, about 15 minutes for IQL and 10 for Filtered BC. Read the data-construction part first, predict the winner from the stitching argument, then run.

units.stopWhen: You can run the inference loop and the calibration inequality from memory, predict a stitching outcome before seeing numbers, and plot a fine-tuning dip with its cause labeled.

fit.note: Hands-on sequence modeling plus Stanford stitching plus Cal-QL and Berkeley fine-tuning slides cover the optional sequence view and required fine-tuning at explain and measure depth.

units.title: Off-policy evaluation targets, importance sampling, weight clipping and effective sample size
outcomes: Derive trajectory and per-decision importance-sampling estimators with their support assumptions.
Implement ordinary, weighted, and per-decision estimates on logged trajectories with a known true value.
Report weight diagnostics (distribution, clipping bias, effective sample size) instead of a bare point estimate.
units.why: Evaluation without interaction stands or falls on the weights. This unit makes every estimator earn its number against a known truth, with the diagnostics that expose a one-trajectory estimate.

next.note: Add models and control variates to cut the variance.
Learn what no weighting can identify.

study.title: Off-policy evaluation via importance sampling
study.locator: Section 3.1 of arXiv:2005.01643v3: the trajectory estimator with its weight product, the per-decision form that drops future weights per reward, and the weighted (self-normalized) variants with their bias-variance tradeoff

study.title: DOPE: the behavior-agnostic protocol and step-wise IS
study.locator: Sections 2 and 3.2 of arXiv:2103.16596v1: evaluation without logged propensities (behavior policy estimated where required) and the split between point-error and ranking metrics; Section 5.1: the IS baseline, self-normalized step-wise importance sampling

study.title: Importance-sampling families before the robust upgrade
study.locator: Section 3.2 of arXiv:1511.03722v3: the ordinary and weighted estimator review that the doubly robust form builds on
study.depth: Read Section 3.2 only here. The doubly robust estimator itself belongs to the next unit.

focus: The evaluation target is the return of a fixed target policy under logged trajectories from a behavior policy. Every estimator here reweights the same logged rewards; they differ only in which weights multiply which reward.

Per-decision weights drop future ratios per reward because a reward cannot depend on later actions. Expectation is unchanged while per-trajectory values change, which is a variance reduction, not a bias fix.

Self-normalized (weighted) estimators divide by the weight sum: lower variance, but biased at finite samples and only consistent. Ordinary estimators are unbiased but can ride on a handful of huge weights.

Effective sample size compresses the weight vector into one number: squared weight sum over sum of squared weights. One dominant weight out of four trajectories gives about 1, and the estimate is then one trajectory wearing a disguise.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, on four logged two-step trajectories with uniform behavior and an always-first-action target (step-one reward 1; step-two reward 1 after the first action and 0 after the second), compute the ordinary estimate (2.0), the per-decision estimate (2.0 via different per-trajectory values), and the effective sample size (1 of 4).
traps: Calling the weighted estimator unbiased because it matched truth once. It is biased at finite samples by construction; matching truth on one dataset is luck, and the bias points toward the behavior policy.

Clipping weights and keeping the unbiasedness claim. Clipping caps variance by adding bias: the clipped weights undercount exactly the trajectories the target policy favors most. Report the clip level and the bias direction instead of hiding them.
Estimating the behavior policy from the same logs and proceeding as if propensities were known. Estimation error enters every weight, and thinly logged actions hide the largest errors.

selfTest.q: Which estimator is unbiased: ordinary or self-normalized? What does the other buy?
selfTest.a: Ordinary is unbiased under support. Self-normalized buys lower variance at the price of finite-sample bias toward the behavior policy; it is consistent, not unbiased.

selfTest.q: In the four-trajectory reproduce case, ordinary and per-decision means agree at 2.0. What differs, and why keep both?
selfTest.a: Per-trajectory values differ (6 versus 8 on the best trajectory) while the mean matches. Per-decision removes future-weight noise per reward, so its variance across datasets is usually lower.

selfTest.q: Weights are 4, 0, 0, 0. What are the ordinary estimate, the self-normalized estimate, and the effective sample size?
selfTest.a: Both estimates equal the first trajectory's return (ordinary mean 4 times return over 4; self-normalized return over weight sum 4). Effective sample size is 1 of 4: a single-trajectory estimate.

selfTest.q: The logging system stored no propensities. What changes in the IS pipeline?
selfTest.a: Fit a behavior-policy model first and use estimated ratios, following the behavior-agnostic protocol. Every weight now carries model error, so support diagnostics matter more, not less.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: ordinary, weighted, and per-decision estimates on logged trajectories from a small MDP with a computable true value, with weight-distribution plots, clipping comparisons, and effective-sample-size diagnostics calibrated against simulator truth.
units.stopWhen: Your hand estimates match code on the four-trajectory case, and you refuse to report any IS number without its weight diagnostics attached.

fit.note: The offline survey plus the DR review section and the DOPE protocol cover IS families and diagnostics at derive depth; the calibrated estimator comparison goes to the mini-project.

units.title: Direct, model-based, doubly robust and Fitted Q Evaluation estimators
outcomes: Derive the doubly robust estimator as model plus importance-weighted residual, with its either-side correctness condition.
Implement Fitted Q Evaluation as iterated supervised regression and compare it with IS estimates against a known truth.
Judge estimators by rank correlation and selection regret, not by one point error.
units.why: Weights alone are too noisy and models alone are too trusting. This unit combines them, then measures estimators the way they are actually used: to rank and select policies.

next.note: Use these estimators for selection where support allows it.
Reserve online truth for auditing these estimates.

study.title: The doubly robust estimator and its variance analysis
study.locator: Sections 1-3 of arXiv:1511.03722v3: the bandit estimator with Equation 8, the sequential extension, unbiasedness when either the behavior policy is known or the model is correct, and the variance analysis

study.title: FQE inside constrained batch policy learning
study.locator: Algorithm 3 of arXiv:1903.08738v1: the iterated target with supervised regression per round; read with the surrounding section on the three estimator families (importance weighting, direct methods, doubly robust)

study.title: DOPE: ranking metrics and the method comparison
study.locator: Sections 3.2 and 4-5 of arXiv:2103.16596v1: absolute error versus rank correlation and selection regret, the FQE, DR, and IS implementations compared, and Figure 7 with the reported scatter of estimate against ground truth

focus: Doubly robust adds an importance-weighted residual onto a model prediction: when the model is right the residual averages out, and when the weights are right the residual fixes the model. Either side being correct keeps the estimate unbiased; neither side rescues missing support.

FQE never touches a weight: it regresses a Q-function onto targets built with the target policy's own actions, round after round. Its error is Bellman error plus function-approximation error plus coverage error, compounded over iterations.

The three families trade differently: weighting is unbiased but noisy, direct methods are quiet but biased by model error, and doubly robust inherits the better side per state when at least one side is right.

Selection needs ordering, not accuracy: a biased estimator that ranks policies correctly selects well with a bad point error, while an unbiased but noisy one can pick a loser. The benchmark reports both, and the ranking metrics decide.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the bandit doubly robust form and the FQE target, then evaluate one logged bandit pair with ratio 2, reward 1, and a model that predicts reward 0.6 for every action: model alone 0.6, IS alone 2.0, doubly robust 1.4.
traps: Claiming double robustness against bad models and bad coverage at once. The guarantee needs one correct side; an unsupported action breaks the weight side and an unverifiable region breaks the model side together.

Iterating FQE many rounds to squeeze the regression loss. Each round fits the previous round's errors too, so late iterations can compound model bias; monitor selection metrics across rounds, not just training loss.
Reporting the smallest absolute error as the best selector. Rank correlation and regret measure the selection job; a low-error estimator that inverts two close policies fails it.

selfTest.q: When is the doubly robust estimator unbiased?
selfTest.a: When either the behavior policy (hence the weights) is known or the model is correct. One correct side suffices; both wrong means no guarantee. With both sides estimated, the paper's claim is asymptotic: either correctly specified side gives consistency.

selfTest.q: Ratio 2, reward 1, model value 0.6. What do the model, IS, and doubly robust estimates give?
selfTest.a: Model 0.6, IS 2.0, doubly robust 0.6 + 2(1 - 0.6) = 1.4. The residual correction pulls the model toward the weighted evidence without inheriting its full variance.

selfTest.q: Write the FQE target for one transition.
selfTest.a: Immediate cost plus discounted next value under the evaluated policy's own action, regressed with supervised learning each round until the iteration budget runs out.

selfTest.q: Two estimators: A has half the absolute error of B but ranks the top two policies backwards. Which selects better?
selfTest.a: B, if its ranking is right: selection pays regret on the chosen policy, and the inverted top pair is exactly what regret punishes. Report rank correlation and regret alongside error.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: FQE on logged data compared with importance-sampling estimates against the simulator truth, plus a doubly robust estimate on the same logs, judged by absolute error, rank correlation, and selection regret.
units.stopWhen: Your hand doubly robust number matches code, your FQE loop beats IS on ranking while you can still name its bias source, and every estimator you report carries all three metrics.

fit.note: The DR and FQE papers plus the DOPE protocol cover direct, robust, and fitted estimators with selection metrics at derive depth; the head-to-head comparison goes to the mini-project.

units.title: Unsupported actions, impossible counterfactuals and offline model selection
outcomes: Prove a counterfactual impossible from support alone, before any estimator runs.
Select policies with rank correlation and regret on held-out logged data, never on hidden online returns.
State what an offline study can and cannot establish about deployment.
units.why: The most expensive offline mistake is a confident claim about an action nobody ever took. This unit makes unsupported mean unsupported, and selection honest.

next.note: Turn the support boundary into deployment guards.
Carry sealed held-out evaluation into reward-model release gates.

study.title: Lecture 17: the counterfactual question
study.locator: PDF pp. 10-11: training data versus what the policy wants to do, and why unseen actions have no honest offline answer

study.title: DOPE: selection protocol with reserved ground truth
study.locator: Sections 3.1-3.2 of arXiv:2103.16596v1: task properties that stress coverage, the policy pools with values from at least 1000 episodes each, and rank correlation plus regret as the selection metrics

study.title: Evaluation and benchmarks without online access
study.locator: Section 6.1 of arXiv:2005.01643v3: how offline work should be evaluated and benchmarked, read as the constraints your selection procedure must satisfy

focus: Support is a yes-or-no question per state and action: if the logging policy never takes an action there, its importance weight is undefined, not large. No estimator, robust or fitted, manufactures the missing outcome.

Thin support is the quantitative sibling: weights exist but concentrate on a few trajectories, so estimates inherit their noise. Report the concentration; the previous unit's diagnostics are the evidence.

Offline model selection ranks candidates on held-out logged data with rank correlation and regret. Online returns, including benchmark ground-truth values, audit the procedure after the fact and must never guide a choice.
An offline study establishes ordering among supported candidates and bounds under stated assumptions. Deployment safety for unsupported regions is out of scope here; the next unit builds the guards.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, construct a one-state two-action log where the second action never appears, show the target policy that always takes it has an undefined weight, and write the candidate-by-estimator selection table with rank correlation left for the mini-project to fill.
traps: Smoothing the behavior-policy estimate to fix zero support. Adding \(\epsilon\) mass makes the weights finite, but no logged sample ever took that action, so its outcome still never enters the estimate; the number is silently biased, not identified.
Tuning on the benchmark's ground-truth returns while calling the study offline. Reserved truth that guides selection is just online tuning with extra steps; keep it sealed until the audit.
Presenting the selected policy as deployment-safe. Selection picks the best-supported candidate; unsupported regions remain unidentified and need the fallback machinery of the next unit.

selfTest.q: What distinguishes an impossible counterfactual from a hard one?
selfTest.a: Zero support makes the weight undefined, so no weighting estimator exists; thin support gives huge but finite weights, so estimates exist with variance the diagnostics must show.

selfTest.q: Why rank correlation instead of absolute error for selecting among three candidates?
selfTest.a: Selection needs the right order and the right winner. An estimator with larger point errors that orders all three correctly has zero selection regret; error alone cannot see that.

selfTest.q: The benchmark ships ground-truth values from 1000-plus episodes. When may you open them?
selfTest.a: After selection is frozen, to audit the estimators and the procedure. Opening them earlier turns the study into online selection wearing an offline label.

selfTest.q: Your estimator ranks every candidate correctly but every point estimate is 30 percent low. Deploy?
selfTest.a: Selection succeeded but the level is unknown, so any threshold-based safety claim still fails. Ranking does not certify absolute performance.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: one exposed support-mismatch failure with the undefined weight written out, plus candidate selection by rank correlation and regret with online returns sealed until the audit.
units.stopWhen: You can exhibit an undefined weight on demand, run a sealed selection procedure, and state in writing what your study does not establish.

fit.note: The counterfactual framing plus the DOPE selection protocol cover unsupported actions and offline selection at explain and measure depth; the sealed procedure goes to the mini-project.

units.title: Normalization consistency, abstention and fallback, and online audit of estimators
outcomes: Apply one frozen normalization from logged data through deployment, with its version recorded.
Define a support-based abstention rule with a fallback policy and a data-collection trigger.
Run an online audit of the section estimators against simulator truth after selection is frozen.
units.why: Offline work ends in a deployment decision, not a leaderboard number. This unit turns support limits into running guards: consistent preprocessing, abstention with fallback, and an audit that cannot leak into selection.

next.note: Collect the triggered data with identified dynamics models.
Compare this abstention rule with fallback replanning under a learned model.

study.title: Minari dataset standards and basic usage
study.locator: Dataset Standards: observation and action spaces, episode and step records, and versioned dataset ids; Basic Usage (https://minari.farama.org/content/basic_usage/): iterating episodes with their recorded spaces (pages read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the standards as a contract your pipeline must satisfy: the spaces and version you train against are the spaces and version you deploy against.

study.title: Homework 1: the normalized interface
study.locator: Environment section: 4-D normalized observations with the target position action in [0, 1]; Problems 1 and 3: the same interface under cloning and under DAgger aggregation

study.title: Control Laboratory: the offline-data stretch
study.locator: Stretch goals: add offline data with off-policy estimates calibrated against simulator truth

focus: Fit every normalization statistic once on the logged data, freeze it, and apply the identical transform at deployment. Refitting on deployment batches or normalizing splits separately silently moves the support boundary your earlier diagnostics certified.

Abstention needs a numeric rule: a support or density test on the state-action pair that routes failures to a fallback policy (for example the cloning baseline on supported regions) and logs the event as a data-collection trigger.

The fallback policy is itself a claim that needs support evidence: it is only safer where its own training distribution covers the abstention region, so characterize its coverage too instead of assuming safety.

Online ground truth audits estimators after selection is frozen. The audit compares importance and fitted-value estimates against simulator returns on held-out policies; nothing it reveals may change a choice.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the three-part deployment checklist (frozen normalization with version, abstention rule with fallback and trigger, sealed audit table), then run it on your Flappy Bird or CartPole policy with one unsupported region demonstrated.
traps: Normalizing with running deployment statistics. The transform becomes a function of the deployment stream, so training and deployment see different mappings and the support test certifies nothing.

Treating abstention rate as a safety metric by itself. A policy that abstains everywhere is useless and one that never abstains may be blind; report abstention with fallback return and trigger counts.
Auditing on the selection policies and stopping. The audit must include held-out policies the estimators never saw during selection, or it measures memory instead of generalization.

selfTest.q: Why must normalization statistics be frozen from the logged data?
selfTest.a: The policy and every support diagnostic were certified under one fixed mapping. A refitted mapping moves states across the certified boundary, so earlier coverage claims no longer apply to the deployed inputs.

selfTest.q: State a complete abstention rule in one sentence each for test, fallback, and trigger.
selfTest.a: Test: route to fallback when the pair's support score falls below the threshold set on held-out logged data. Fallback: execute the cloning baseline restricted to supported regions. Trigger: log the event with state, score, and version for the next collection round.

selfTest.q: What may the online audit change?
selfTest.a: Nothing about selection. It scores the frozen estimators against simulator truth and records where they fail; any change it suggests belongs to a new documented study round.

selfTest.q: The fallback is plain behavior cloning. Is the deployed system now safe?
selfTest.a: Only where cloning itself has support evidence. The fallback needs its own coverage characterization over the abstention region; outside that, the system must escalate or stop, not silently proceed.
